# Hoshi-no-Tani — The Valley of Stars

### ▶ [**Play it in your browser →**](https://howarddc.github.io/hoshi-no-tani/)

A late-summer afternoon in a valley that does not exist. Every blade of grass,
every stone in the viaduct, every cloud, and every note of the soundtrack is
**generated by code** — no textures, no 3D models, no audio recordings
anywhere in this repository.

**This repo exists to be taken apart.** The demo arrived as a single
6,184-line HTML file, which is a wonderful thing to look at and a miserable
thing to change. It is now 22 documented modules with an
[AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md), a build system, and checks that catch the mistakes a
rendered frame will not show you. Fork it, point an AI coding agent at it, and
grow it into something of your own.

![The valley: a stone viaduct crossing a river, with a meadow in the foreground](docs/screenshot.jpg)

> **Originally created by [Lentils](https://codepen.io/lentils801), who built it
> with Claude Opus 5 and shared it
> [in this post on X](https://x.com/Lentils80/status/2081136109778538917).**
> That post is where this project came from — watch the video there to see the
> grass move, which a still cannot show you. Everything you see in the demo is
> their work; this fork reorganises it so it is easier to pick up and extend.
> See [Attribution](#attribution-and-licence).

---

## Run it

**Easiest:** open the [live version](https://howarddc.github.io/hoshi-no-tani/).

**On your own machine:** clone the repo and double-click **`dist/index.html`**.
No install, no build, no server — it is a single self-contained file that opens
straight from your filesystem, which is a deliberate property rather than a
happy accident (see [How it fits together](#how-it-fits-together)).

Either way you need an internet connection, since Three.js loads from a CDN.
Give it a few seconds to carve a terrain, grow a meadow and stack some clouds,
then click **Enter the valley**. It opens on the lowest quality preset so it
starts fast anywhere — press **`3`** or **`4`** once you are in and the meadow
fills out properly.

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `W` `A` `S` `D` | Walk |
| `Shift` | Run |
| Mouse | Look — click once to capture the pointer |
| `F` | Toggle flight, then `Space` / `Ctrl` for up and down |
| `T` | Summon the train |
| `C` | Cinematic camera — hands off, it flies itself |
| `H` | Settings panel |
| `P` | Pause |
| `1`–`4` | Quality: low, medium, high, ultra |
| `Esc` | Release the pointer |

Worth doing on your first visit: stand underneath the viaduct and press `T` to
send the train over your head — the valve gear is actually solved, so the rods
move the way real rods move. Press `F` and fly to the cloud deck at 980 m. Then
come back down and stand still in the grass with the sound on, because the wind
you can hear is driven by the same field that is bending the blades in front of
you.

---

## Take it somewhere new

Two ways in, depending on how you like to work. They mix perfectly well.

### With an AI coding agent

Clone the repo, open it in Claude Code, Cursor, or anything similar, and
describe what you want. The agent will find [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) on its own
and pick up:

- **An architecture map** — what each of the 22 modules does and where the
  render pipeline's passes happen.
- **The invariants that are not obvious from reading the code** — the scene
  contract, the fixed render-order ladder, the shared uniform block, and the
  fact that the terrain height function is deliberately written twice (once in
  JavaScript, once in GLSL) and the two must always be changed together.
- **The traps** — including several that cost real hours to find the first
  time, like a table of contents that advertises a section which does not
  exist, and dead configuration flags that look load-bearing but are read by
  nothing.
- **How to verify a change**, which matters here because there is no test
  suite. A rendered frame is the check, and some mistakes (a missing shadow, a
  stale build) look like art direction rather than bugs.

That file was written *from doing the work* rather than as an aspiration — it
records what actually went wrong. Some things to ask for:

```
Add a day/night cycle with a moving sun.
Add rain: particles, darker palette, wet-looking ground.
Put a second village on the far bank of the river.
Give the train a schedule and a station to stop at.
Make the sky colours respond to the sun angle instead of being hand-painted.
```

That last one is the most interesting, and *Move the sun* below explains why.

**One rule to pass on to your agent:** anything under `src/` requires
`python3 tools/build.py` afterwards, or the playable `dist/index.html` goes
stale. CI enforces it, and AGENTS.md says so, but it is the single easiest
thing to forget.

### By hand

Serve the `src/` folder and your changes appear on reload with no build step:

```bash
cd src && python3 -m http.server 8000
```

Open <http://localhost:8000>, edit a file, reload, see it. (Run
`python3 tools/build.py` when you want the double-clickable single file back.)

---

## Five things to change first

### 1. Repaint the whole valley — `src/modules/palette.js`

Every colour in the film is in one object. Change a hex code, reload, done.

```js
export const P = {
  skyZenith:'#4E80B4', skyUpper:'#7BA9CE', ...
  gTip:'#C6D46B', gUpper:'#93B84E', gMid:'#6C9A47', ...
```

Push the grass colours (`gTip`, `gUpper`, `gMid`, `gLow`) toward oranges and
browns for autumn. They flow into the shaders automatically — converted to
linear space and injected into the GLSL as constants when the shaders compile
at startup — so you never touch a shader to recolour anything.

### 2. Move the sun — `src/modules/config.js`

```js
sunElev: 13.5,   // degrees above the horizon
sunAzim: 292.0,  // degrees, 0 = north, increasing toward east
```

Drop `sunElev` to `4` for a raking, nearly-sunset light with very long shadows.
Push it to `45` for a flat midday. Change `sunAzim` to swing the light around
and watch which hillsides catch it.

**A thing worth noticing:** the sky will not follow. It is a *painted* gradient
— hand-picked colours in the palette — not a scattering simulation, so a low
sun under a midday sky looks wrong. That trade is deliberate, and it is much of
why this looks like a film cel instead of a photograph. Making the sky respond
to the sun automatically is a genuinely interesting project, and it is a good
first job to hand an agent: the work is mostly promoting those baked-in
constants to uniforms.

### 3. Go somewhere specific — no file editing needed

```
http://localhost:8000/?cam=-46.5,92.1,180,-8   # spawn point, facing south
http://localhost:8000/?q=3&d=1.4               # ultra preset, dense grass
http://localhost:8000/?post=0                  # post-processing off
```

These work on the [live version](https://howarddc.github.io/hoshi-no-tani/)
too, so a URL is a shareable viewpoint — for instance
[the valley at ultra quality](https://howarddc.github.io/hoshi-no-tani/?q=3&d=1.4).

`x` and `z` are world metres and `heading` is degrees. Note `?d=` is a
**multiplier**, not a percentage — `1.0` is full density, the default is `0.2`.
(The settings slider shows the same value as a percentage, which is worth
knowing before you type `?d=100` and wonder why your browser stopped
responding.)

`?post=0` is worth doing once: it bypasses the bloom, the watercolour softening
and the film print curve to show you the raw render. The difference is
startling, and a good lesson in how much of the "look" of a piece like this is
image processing rather than geometry.

### 4. Change the grass — `src/modules/config.js`

```js
export const RINGS = [
  { chunk:  9,  blades:  89000, near:0,  far:26,  dn:7,  wpx:1.70, hs:1.00 },
  ...
```

Grass is drawn in four concentric rings of decreasing detail. `hs` is height
scale — raise it and you are wading through a hayfield. The comments around
this table explain the density law properly, and are worth reading if you have
wondered how a million-blade meadow runs at all.

### 5. Build something — `src/modules/village.js`

The village uses a small toolkit — `pbox`, `pcyl`, `proof` (a gabled roof) —
that pushes vertices into a buffer. Copy a cottage, move it, change its roof
colour. Two rules: register it with `pushSolid` so you cannot walk through it,
and add it with `addMesh` (below) or it will silently cast no shadow.

## How it fits together

If this is your first time inside a project shaped like this, here is the tour.

### It started as one enormous file

The original was a single 6,184-line HTML file. That is a perfectly reasonable
way to write a demo — self-contained, and it just runs — but it is a hard thing
to *extend*: every change touches the same file, diffs are unreadable, and two
people cannot work on it at once. Neither, in practice, can an agent work on it
comfortably, because the file is larger than most tools want to read at once.

So it is now **22 ES modules** in `src/modules/`, split along boundaries the
original author had already marked with comment banners:

```
config.js  palette.js  math.js  scene-contract.js  glsl.js
terrain.js  sky.js  wind.js  grass.js  river.js  trees.js
viaduct.js  railway.js  village.js  train.js  post.js
walker.js  audio.js  materials.js  field.js  track-ref.js  main.js
```

### But it still has to be one file

Here is the interesting constraint. A browser will happily run an *inline*
`<script type="module">` from a `file://` page — which is why you can
double-click `dist/index.html`. But the moment that script does
`import './terrain.js'`, the browser blocks it: a relative import from a
`file://` page is a same-origin request from an opaque origin, and that is
forbidden.

So splitting into modules would have destroyed the single best property of the
project — that you can double-click it and it works.

The answer is `tools/build.py`: dependency-free Python that concatenates the
modules back into one inline script and writes `dist/index.html`. Source you
can navigate; artifact you can double-click.

```bash
python3 tools/build.py          # rebuild dist/index.html
python3 tools/build.py --check  # verify it is in sync (this is what CI runs)
```

Concatenation is a crude bundling strategy that works here because of an
accident of history: the code *was* one file, so every top-level name is
already unique and the original ordering is known good. The build script
asserts all of that — unique names, no import cycles, no imported name that its
module does not actually export — and refuses to emit a bundle if any of it
breaks. A loud failure is much cheaper than a subtly wrong bundle, and it is
the sort of guard rail that matters most when something else is doing the
editing.

### One rule you have to know

Whether a mesh casts a shadow is decided by one thing: whether it carries a
depth material. Forget it and your new building silently stops casting — and
under a sun 13.5° above the horizon, where shadow carries most of the shape,
that reads as a lighting bug and sends you hunting in the wrong place.

So nothing is added to the scene directly. Everything goes through a factory
where the decision is a **required argument**:

```js
addMesh(scene, mesh, someDepthMaterial);  // casts a shadow
addMesh(scene, mesh, NO_CAST);            // deliberately does not
```

You cannot skip the decision, only make it. Worth stealing for your own
projects: when a mistake is silent, make it impossible rather than documenting
it.

---

## Worth reading the source for

The comments explain *why*, including approaches that were tried and rejected —
rarer and more useful than comments explaining what.

- **A million blades of grass that actually runs.** The near rings are drawn
  twice — once with colour writes off, purely to lay down depth — so the
  hardware discards the ~30 blades of overdraw stacked at every pixel before
  doing any shading.
- **One number chosen for its instruction count.** The grass density exponent
  is 1.5 rather than 1.45, because at exactly 1.5 the shader computes it in
  three single-cycle instructions instead of calling `pow()` — and it runs on
  roughly 12 million vertices a frame.
- **Cloud shadows for one texture fetch.** The coverage field is thirteen
  octaves of warped noise. Rather than evaluate that per pixel in six shaders,
  it is baked once per frame into a small map.
- **The CPU and GPU never disagree.** The terrain height function is written
  twice, once in each language, deliberately mirroring each other — so your
  feet, the grass roots, the camera and the rendered ground always agree about
  where the hill is.
- **The soundtrack is synthesised from nothing.** Noise buffers, oscillators,
  filters, and a reverb whose impulse response is generated from decaying
  noise. The wind you hear is sampled from the field that bends the grass.

---

## Requirements

Nothing to install. A browser with WebGL2 (any current one), an internet
connection for the Three.js CDN, and Python 3 if you want the build script or a
local server.
